content:
Experimental work in the project library indicates that the explicitness of written corrective feedback (WCF) shapes both immediate revision and durability. The same trial found that cognitive load during revision after direct corrections on grammatical errors was significantly lower than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (Bonilla López et al., 2018).

Automated feedback occupies a different position in the evidence base. Automated feedback highlights rather than corrects errors (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). Teacher feedback addressed more error types than automated feedback, although assignment differences may have influenced this comparison (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). Comparisons of ChatGPT and Grammarly found that ChatGPT maintained high precision across prompts (94–98%) versus Grammarly's 85%, while recall rose from 10% to 55% as prompts became more sophisticated (Luo et al., 2025). Teachers using Grammarly as a complement still addressed both global and local concerns, with no division of labour (Koltovskaia, 2022).

Evidence on learner response is largely naturalistic. A 16-week naturalistic case study of two Chinese students found that the highly engaged learner outperformed the moderately engaged learner in responding to both teacher and automated feedback and in improving her text (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). In an integrated approach combining automated, peer, and teacher feedback, most of 33 students actively engaged and the approach promoted behavioural, affective, and cognitive engagement and thoughtful revisions (Zhang & Hyland, 2021). A synthesis of 50 naturalistic classroom studies identified teacher practices, learner responses, stakeholder beliefs, and motivation and emotions as major themes (Mao et al., 2024).

sentences: Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing has expanded across experimental, naturalistic, and review literatures, addressing teacher-provided, peer-provided, and automated feedback.
This review synthesizes the library around three themes: the accuracy effects of feedback type, learner engagement and revision behaviour, and the affordances and limits of automated feedback.
A synthesis paragraph then states the gap the present review addresses.
Experimental evidence indicates that comprehensive feedback forms differ in their durability.

In a study with 139 low-intermediate EFL writers randomly assigned to four feedback conditions and a self-correction control, direct corrections and metalinguistic codes both enhanced immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy during revision, yet a long-term advantage four weeks after feedback was evident only for direct corrections (Bonilla López et al., 2018).

The same trial found that cognitive load during revision after direct corrections on grammatical errors was significantly lower than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (Bonilla López et al., 2018).

This suggests that the explicitness of feedback interacts with processing effort, although cognitive load was measured through self-report rather than an online physiological measure (Bonilla López et al., 2018).
Engagement research shows that feedback effects depend on how learners process comments.

A 16-week naturalistic case study of two Chinese students found that the highly engaged learner outperformed the moderately engaged learner in responding to both teacher and automated feedback and in improving her text (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).
Teacher feedback addressed more error types than automated feedback, although assignment differences may have influenced this comparison (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).

In an integrated approach combining automated, peer, and teacher feedback, most of 33 students actively engaged and the approach promoted behavioural, affective, and cognitive engagement and thoughtful revisions (Zhang & Hyland, 2021).
Automated feedback highlights rather than corrects errors (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).

Comparisons of ChatGPT and Grammarly found that ChatGPT maintained high precision across prompts (94–98%) versus Grammarly's 85%, while recall rose from 10% to 55% as prompts became more sophisticated (Luo et al., 2025).
Teachers using Grammarly as a complement still addressed both global and local concerns, with no division of labour (Koltovskaia, 2022).
A synthesis of 50 naturalistic classroom studies identified teacher practices, learner responses, stakeholder beliefs, and motivation and emotions as major themes (Mao et al., 2024).
Taken together, the literature establishes that feedback type shapes accuracy and that engagement mediates uptake.
However, direct comparisons of teacher, peer, and automated feedback on revision behaviour and engagement within a single design remain unexamined.
The present review addresses this gap by synthesizing evidence across all three feedback sources.

verifications.explanation: The source states verbatim: "ChatGPT remained consistently high in precision regardless of prompts, being 94%, 98% and 94% respectively for GPT-P1, GPT-P2 and GPT-P3, higher than Grammarly (85%). In contrast, the recall of ChatGPT considerably improved across prompts, with that of GPT-P1, GPT-P2 and GPT-P3 being 10%, 33% and 55% respectively." Table 1 confirms totals of 94/98/94 precision for ChatGPT versus 85 for Grammarly, and recall 10/33/55. The claim's precision range 94–98% matches the three ChatGPT values, Grammarly's 85% matches, and the recall endpoints 10% and 55% match the least and most sophisticated prompts. The central assertion (ChatGPT's precision across prompts exceeded Grammarly's) and the peripheral assertions (the specific values and the recall increase) are all supported.

The central assertion (majority of the 33 students actively engaged) is supported by "the majority of students actively engaged with this integrated approach"; the peripheral assertions about the three-feedback integration, the promotion of behavioural/affective/cognitive engagement, and thoughtful revisions are each supported by the same abstract sentence. No assertion is contradicted; the paper's caveat that some students failed to engage is consistent with "most" rather than "all".
